text.p: Peter Shirtcliffe, chairman of New Zealand's largest company, Telecom Corp, has said the Alliance party and its leader Jim Anderton are "control freaks" who would hurt business if they became part of government.

Shirtcliffe also said in an interview in Sydney that any Alliance attempt in government to cut Telecom's prices and profits would reverberate throughout the business community and discourage competition.
Anderton has said his party would force Telecom to cut residential line charges by 30 percent if it won power in the October 12 election.
"Mr Anderton has decided that he will focus on Telecom as some sort of icon in relation to his own somewhat intrusive brand of socialism," Shirtcliffe told Reuters.

"Telecom may be the icon for Mr Anderton to say we're going to control their profits. What I'd say is -- 'it may be us today, it will be you tomorrow' -- that's what I'd say to every other business," Shirtcliffe said.
"It isn't just about Telecom. It's about a whole philosophy of control and regulation. These guys can't help themselves," he said. "These guys are control freaks."
Shirtcliffe said New Zealand had come out of an era of being run by control freaks in the mid 1980s which had retarded growth and New Zealanders knew they could not go back a second time.
"Kiwis (New Zealanders) no longer want that environment."
Shirtcliffe said any attempt by the Alliance or any other party in government to use the so-called kiwi share to cut residential line charges or Telecom's profits would be counterproductive.
It would restrict competition and was likely to be part of a wider re-regulatory push that would hurt business.

When Telecom was privatised the government continued to hold a "kiwi share" which forced Telecom to keep residential line charge increases below the inflation rate and to keep local residential calls free.
"The kiwi share's a two way deal. It's a contract." Shirtcliffe said, adding he did not believe Anderton understood how the kiwi share worked.

"If a politician and a group of politicians want to come and fiddle with the environment, I think you've got to take it as a given that they will be dealing not just with Telecom, but with the business environment generally," he said.
Telecom currently cross-subsidised its residential customers by charging higher rates for its business customers and any cut in residential rates could see business rates rise.
Lower residential rates would also discourage competition in the residential market, Shirtcliffe said.
"If you reduce those local rental prices, how is anybody going to provide a competitive service," he said.
The Alliance has had about 15 percent support in recent polls, while the centre-left Labor and economic nationalist New Zealand First parties have each had support of about 20 percent.

The ruling centre-right National government has had about 35-40 percent support, insufficient to govern in its own right under the new proportional voting system being used for the first time on October 12.
A centre-left coalition government is seen a possibility.

Shirtcliffe told a business luncheon in Sydney on Friday that NZ$20 billion of Australian investment in New Zealand was at serious risk if populist parties like Anderton's Alliance and Winston Peters' NZ First won government.
Peters later said Shirtcliffe was the corporate face of the politics of greed and should stay out of politics.
